newsitem.title: FRANCE: RUGBY UNION-FRANCE DREAM OF HISTORIC FAREWELL TO PARC.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-FRANCE DREAM OF HISTORIC FAREWELL TO PARC.

text.p: France dream of making history with a rare grand slam on Saturday but fear Scotland might spoil their emotional farewell to Parc des Princes.
France, who will appear for the last time in the Five Nations at the concrete oval which has been linked to their destiny for the last 24 years, are only 80 minutes away from an unexpected triumph.

Never before in the tournament had France lost so many key players but despite missing the likes of Philippe St Andre, Emile Ntamack and Olivier Roumat they won their first three matches and need just another win to achieve their first grand slam in 10 years.

All four of France's previous clean sweeps, in 1968, 1977, 1981 and 1987, were completed on foreign territory. Now they can do it on home soil and earn a last lap of honour at the Parc before starting a new adventure at Stade de France.
From next year, France will entertain their guests in the high-tech, 80,000-capacity arena currently being built in the suburb of St Denis for the 1998 soccer World Cup finals.

"We're entering a new era", sighed French coach Jean-Claude Skrela, who so often delighted Parc des Princes when he played alongside Jean-Pierre Rives in a formidable back row. "Now everything has to be gigantic. The Parc is getting too small, so we'll have to go to Stade de France."

Skrela, who lost both half-backs and one prop in the build-up to Saturday's crucial clash, retains clear memories of his 1977 grand slam and urged his players not to squander the opportunity offered to them.
"I had never won anything before that day (of 1977) and I realised that I had won a title at last, something nobody would forget," he recalled. "I was right because people still talk about it now."

Injuries have once again forced the French selectors to reshuffle their team. Pau fly-half David Aucagne takes over from the injured Alain Penaud while Guy Accoceberry replaces Philippe Carbonneau at scrum-half.
Brive prop Didier Casadei wins his first cap in place of Christian Califano, who was automatically suspended after being sent off for punching an opponent in a league game at the weekend.
Scotland, who won their last two Five Nations' matches against France, will rely on the team who convincingly beat Ireland in their last match.

"The fact that France will go for the grand slam is good news to us," said skipper Rob Wainwright, who also remembers that Scotland would have beaten France in the 1995 World Cup without a brilliant Ntamack try in injury time.
"The pressure will be on their shoulders and we will be able to concentrate on playing a good match," he added.
Wainwright knows what he is is talking about as Scotland were in France's situation in last year's tournament, when their hopes of a grand slam were shattered by an English victory at Murrayfield.
"Everybody was expecting so much from us," he said. "We we were thinking too much about the grand slam and we lost."
Skrela said the keys to a French win were humility and a tight defence.

"We must be humble and give Scotland respect if we want to avoid bitter disappointment," he said. "Before trying anything else, the players must defend for the whole match. Against a team like Scotland, who keep going for it and never give up, that's the only solution."
France would make a costly mistake, Skrela added, by believing that they had done the hardest part with their sensational finish for a 23-20 win at Twickenham on March 1.
"We might have won three matches already but we haven't won anything yet," he said. "To get a title, you have to win the final and the final is now."
